nodes.label: Daniel K Richter
nodes.date_label: “War and Culture: The Iroquois Experience” (1983) · The Ordeal of the Longhouse (1992) · Facing East from Indian Country (2001)

nodes.label: Jack P Greene
nodes.date_label: Peripheries and Center (1986) · Pursuits of Happiness (1988) · Atlantic History: A Critical Appraisal: co-edited with Philip D. Morgan (2008)
nodes.description: A historian of colonial British America and comparative Atlantic history. In his 2019 conversation with Miguel Dantas da Cruz, Greene explains why comparison should attend to differences as well as connections, and why an Atlantic frame may need wider hemispheric reach. His emphasis on colonial autonomy is therefore presented alongside an explicit warning about the costs of expansion to Indigenous peoples and enslaved Africans.

nodes.label: C. Vann Woodward
nodes.date_label: Origins of the New South (1951) · Reunion and Reaction (1951) · The Strange Career of Jim Crow (1955) · “The Future of the Past”: presidential address delivered (1969)
nodes.description: A historian of the American South whose work challenged accounts of an unchanging racial order. Bertram Wyatt-Brown’s substantive memorial presents The Strange Career of Jim Crow as an argument about the historical formation of segregation, while noting later revisions and declining scholarly influence. Woodward’s own presidential address argues that historians should expose anachronisms and mediate between aspirations and historical constraints. The entry keeps that civic role distinct from endorsing a consoling national past or treating a once influential interpretation as settled.

nodes.label: Jeremy Black
nodes.date_label: The English Press in the Eighteenth Century (1987) · A Military Revolution? (1991) · Rethinking Military History (2004) · The British Seaborne Empire (2004)
nodes.description: A historian of warfare, British politics and the uses of history. The existing participant-editor reading of the military-revolution debate places him among critics of its conventional chronology, emphasizing continuity and later change. In his own written Sonshi interview he describes a comparative military history that challenges a restricted Western frame and resists a rigid separation between strategy and policy. Both arguments are scoped: the first is mediated by Clifford J. Rogers, the second is Black’s self-description, and neither establishes a single settled explanation of global military change.

nodes.label: Niall Ferguson
nodes.date_label: The Pity of War (1998) · Empire: How Britain Made the Modern World (2003) · The Shock of the Global: four-editor collection (2010)
nodes.description: A historian of war, finance and empire whose work makes counterfactual comparison explicit. These judgments remain Ferguson’s claims, including their chosen comparisons and values; the entry does not adopt them as settled verdicts on war or empire. His co-editorship of The Shock of the Global is separately credited.

row.context: Reorients early-American narratives around Native communities’ strategies and experiences of colonial encounters.
row.works: “War and Culture: The Iroquois Experience” (1983); The Ordeal of the Longhouse (1992); Facing East from Indian Country (2001; paperback 2003).

row.context: Uses contextual reconstruction while acknowledging that surviving sources cannot give transparent access to a Native subject’s experience.
row.works: “War and Culture: The Iroquois Experience” (1983); The Ordeal of the Longhouse (1992); Facing East from Indian Country (2001; paperback 2003).

row.context: Investigates soldiers’ combat endurance through letters, diaries, comradeship and reputational obligations.
row.works: The Struggle for Equality (1964; later anniversary edition with a new preface); Battle Cry of Freedom (1988); For Cause and Comrades (1997).

row.context: Examines volunteer soldiers’ political commitments and their competing understandings of national purpose.
row.works: The Struggle for Equality (1964; later anniversary edition with a new preface); Battle Cry of Freedom (1988); For Cause and Comrades (1997).

row.context: Treats masculine status as relational and historically produced across home, work and male associations.
row.works: “What Should Historians Do with Masculinity?” (1994); A Man’s Place (1999; paperback 2007); Manliness and Masculinities in Nineteenth-Century Britain (2005).

row.context: Advocates historical context, debated interpretations and bounded analogy as resources for democratic citizenship.
row.works: “What Should Historians Do with Masculinity?” (1994); A Man’s Place (1999; paperback 2007); Manliness and Masculinities in Nineteenth-Century Britain (2005).

row.context: Criticizes the privileging of invariants and permanence when it excludes events, individual subjects and historical change.
row.works: L’Histoire en miettes (1987); La marche des idées (2003); Le pari biographique (2005; paperback with new preface 2011); “L’histoire entre la guerre des mémoires et la Justice” (2017).

row.context: Distinguishes work of memory, historical explanation and judicial judgment while examining their overlapping claims on the past.
row.works: L’Histoire en miettes (1987); La marche des idées (2003); Le pari biographique (2005; paperback with new preface 2011); “L’histoire entre la guerre des mémoires et la Justice” (2017).

row.context: Connects colonial sociological measurement and sexual classification to the production of racial hierarchy.
row.works: The Amateur and the Professional (1986; paperback 2002); “Orientalist Sociology and the Creation of Colonial Sexualities” (2000); Prostitution, Race and Politics (2003); Gender and Empire, editor (2004; paperback 2007).

row.context: Develops comparison attentive to differences and interconnections, while considering a wider hemispheric frame.

row.context: Warns that accounts of negotiated colonial autonomy must confront the costs of settler expansion to Indigenous peoples and enslaved Africans.
row.works: Peripheries and Center (1986); Pursuits of Happiness (1988); Atlantic History: A Critical Appraisal, co-edited with Philip D. Morgan (publisher release listing 2008; also cited as 2009).

row.works: Origins of the New South (1951); Reunion and Reaction (1951; later editions with new prefaces); The Strange Career of Jim Crow (1955; repeatedly revised); “The Future of the Past,” presidential address (delivered 1969).
